q: Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis in adults < 50 years?
a: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin

q: Empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis in adults > 50 years or immunocompromised?
a: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin + Ampicillin (to cover Listeria)

q: Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)?
a: Streptococcus pneumoniae

q: Empiric outpatient treatment for CAP in healthy adult with no comorbidities?
a: Amoxicillin OR Doxycycline OR Macrolide (if local pneumococcal resistance is < 25%)

q: Empiric inpatient (non-ICU) treatment for CAP?
a: Fluoroquinolone (Respiratory) OR (Beta-lactam + Macrolide)

q: CURB-65 criteria components?
a: Confusion, Urea > 20 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥ 30, Blood pressure (SBP < 90 or DBP ≤ 60), Age ≥ 65

q: Treatment for latent Tuberculosis infection (LTBI)?
a: Isoniazid + Rifapentine weekly for 3 months OR Rifampin daily for 4 months OR Isoniazid + Rifampin daily for 3 months.

q: Most specific test for diagnosing syphilis?
a: FTA-ABS or TPPA (Treponemal tests)

q: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction symptoms and management?
a: Fever, myalgias, headache within 24 hours of starting syphilis treatment. Management is supportive (NSAIDs), continue antibiotics.

q: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen and duration?
a: Tenofovir + Emtricitabine + (Raltegravir or Dolutegravir) for 28 days.

q: CD4 count < 200/mm<sup>3</sup> prophylaxis in HIV?
a: TMP-SMX for Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP)

q: CD4 count < 100/mm<sup>3</sup> and positive Toxoplasma IgG prophylaxis in HIV?
a: TMP-SMX for Toxoplasma gondii

q: Diagnosis of HIV in adults?
a: HIV-1/2 Antigen/Antibody combo immunoassay, followed by HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation immunoassay if positive.

q: Primary syphilis presentation?
a: Painless chancre (ulcer) with indurated borders and painless regional lymphadenopathy.

q: Genital ulcer disease: Painful vesicles on erythematous base?
a: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)

q: Genital ulcer disease: Painful, purulent ulcer with ragged edges and painful lymphadenopathy (buboes)?
a: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi)

q: Genital ulcer disease: Painless, beefy-red ulcer with bleeding and no lymphadenopathy?
a: Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis, Klebsiella granulomatis)

q: Treatment for uncomplicated cystitis in women?
a: Nitrofurantoin (5 days), TMP-SMX (3 days), or Fosfomycin (single dose).

q: Treatment for pyelonephritis?
a: Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin (oral if stable), or IV Ceftriaxone/Ampicillin-Sulbactam (if hospitalized).

q: Next best step in management for suspected infective endocarditis?
a: Three sets of blood cultures drawn from different sites BEFORE initiating empiric antibiotics, followed by Echocardiogram.

q: Empiric treatment for native valve infective endocarditis?
a: Vancomycin (covers MRSA, Strep, and Enterococcus).

q: Prophylaxis for infective endocarditis prior to dental procedures is indicated for whom?
a: Prosthetic heart valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, completely repaired CHD within 6 months, repaired CHD with residual defects, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy.

q: Tick-borne disease presenting with fever, headache, myalgias, and thrombocytopenia/leukopenia, without a rash?
a: Ehrlichiosis or Anaplasmosis (Treat with Doxycycline)

q: Classic triad of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF)?
a: Fever, headache, and petechial rash (starts on wrists/ankles and spreads centrally).

q: Treatment for Lyme disease (early localized)?
a: Doxycycline (Amoxicillin or Cefuroxime for children < 8 years or pregnant women).

q: Malaria prophylaxis for Chloroquine-resistant areas?
a: Atovaquone-proguanil, Doxycycline, or Mefloquine.

q: Treatment for severe Clostridioides difficile infection (WBC > 15,000 or Cr > 1.5)?
a: Oral Vancomycin or Oral Fidaxomicin.

q: Diagnostic test for Osteomyelitis?
a: MRI (most sensitive), followed by bone biopsy with culture (gold standard for targeted therapy).

q: Common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease?
a: Salmonella species and Staphylococcus aureus.

q: Patient with neutropenic fever (ANC < 500). Empiric therapy?
a: Antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Cefepime, Meropenem, Piperacillin-Tazobactam).

q: Treatment for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis?
a: Penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM single dose.

q: Presentation of babesiosis?
a: Fever, hemolytic anemia (jaundice, dark urine), thrombocytopenia. Blood smear shows Maltese cross.

q: Vector and tick species for Lyme disease?
a: Ixodes scapularis (deer tick).

q: Typical CSF findings in viral meningitis?
a: Normal/mildly elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, normal/mildly elevated protein.

q: Typical CSF findings in bacterial meningitis?
a: Elevated opening pressure, PMN pleocytosis, low glucose (< 40 mg/dL), highly elevated protein.

q: Patient from Southwestern US (e.g., Arizona) with pneumonia, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias. Diagnosis?
a: Coccidioidomycosis.

q: Ohio/Mississippi River valley exposure (bat/bird droppings, caves), presenting with pulmonary symptoms and hilar lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
a: Histoplasmosis.

q: Most common cause of prosthetic joint infection within the first 3 months of surgery?
a: Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

q: Most common cause of delayed (3-12 months) prosthetic joint infection?
a: Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative Staph).

q: Empiric treatment for septic arthritis (Gram stain pending or negative)?
a: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone.

q: Animal bite (dog/cat) treatment?
a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (covers Pasteurella multocida and oral anaerobes).

q: Human bite treatment?
a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (covers Eikenella corrodens and anaerobes).

q: When to add steroids (dexamethasone) in suspected bacterial meningitis?
a: Administer with or just before the first dose of antibiotics (proven beneficial for S. pneumoniae).

q: Painful, grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. Diagnosis and treatment?
a: Herpes Zoster (Shingles); treat with Valacyclovir or Acyclovir.

q: Cutaneous anthrax presentation?
a: Painless ulcer with a black eschar and significant surrounding edema.

q: Empiric treatment for hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) or ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)?
a: Antipseudomonal coverage (e.g., Cefepime) + MRSA coverage (e.g., Vancomycin).

q: Bloody diarrhea with no fever, possible history of consuming undercooked ground beef. Diagnosis?
a: EHEC (Enterohemorrhagic E. coli, O157:H7). Avoid antibiotics due to risk of HUS.

q: Cause of "rice-water" diarrhea and severe dehydration?
a: Vibrio cholerae.

q: Classic presentation of Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) in HIV?
a: CD4 < 50; systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), diarrhea, and elevated ALP.

q: Secondary syphilis presentation?
a: Diffuse maculopapular rash involving palms and soles, condyloma lata, generalized lymphadenopathy.
